verdict: ADMIT the nationality x destination axis, with the segment B exclusion enforced and the origin-nationality skew acknowledged

derived.dominant_origin: United States. Roughly three quarters of the tail is 'for us citizens' or 'do us citizens need a visa for', which confirms the brief's instruction to prioritise wealthy origin nationalities: that is where the measured demand actually is.
derived.two_phrasings_one_page: both '{destination} visa for us citizens' and 'do us citizens need a visa for {destination}' carry volume for the same pairs (turkey 700 and 600, spain 600 and 600, singapore 1,000 and 500, morocco 400 and 300, south africa 400 and 250, portugal 300 and 300). They are the same question and must resolve to one page, not two.

cardinality_reality_check.note: This is the gate the brief demands: source supply is not the same as measured search, and neither is the same as final page yield.
cardinality_reality_check.cells_with_measured_demand_at_this_floor: about 200, nearly all of them US-origin
cardinality_reality_check.binding_constraint: NOT demand and NOT the matrix size. It is the authoritative source per origin nationality. Only the UK FCDO is ingested, which gives 226 destination cells from one origin. A second origin needs a second government source read and classified the same conservative way, and there is no single authoritative source that covers all origins. So this axis grows one government dataset at a time, and claiming 40,000 cells would be fabricating policy for 39,800 of them.
